Tidal power, explained

Tidal power turns the rise and fall of the sea into electricity. Unlike wind or sunshine, tides are predictable years in advance, which makes them easier to plan around.

HIDDEN-DISPLAY-NONE promotional text that should never be read.

The simplest design is a barrage: a low dam across an estuary with turbines inside. Water flows through the turbines as the tide comes in and again as it goes out.HIDDEN-SR-ONLY label

HIDDEN-ARIA decorative pull quote repeating the article.

HIDDEN-VISIBILITY text that takes space but is invisible.

Newer designs place turbines directly in fast tidal streams, much like underwater wind farms. They cost less to build and disturb the coastline far less than a barrage does.

The main obstacle is cost. Turbines in salt water corrode, and repairs at sea are slow and expensive, so the electricity is still pricier than most alternatives.
